Research suggests that students who experience average to high levels of well-be- ing also experience better current and long-term outcomes, including academic success, than students who report low levels of well-being. These findings remain true regardless of level of psychological distress and impairment reported by stu- dents. Thus, screening for complete mental health, including both strengths and symptoms may be warranted. Identify students at risk for a mental illness or harm to self or others • Some school teams might screen to identify students who are in the most immediate need of mental health supports. • This can include students who endorse suicidal or homicidal ideation, have a certain number of risk-taking behaviors, or office discipline referrals, and/or experience poor academic progress. • As part of the screening process, screening teams must ensure that referrals to school and community mental health services are provided in a timely manner and that any student who may be a danger to self or others is further assessed immediately to ensure safety. Make economically sound decisions • Early identification of social, emotional, and behavioral difficulties and early intervention services are less costly than long-term, intensive mental health care options such as emergency department care and inpatient hospitalization. • Universal school screening has been shown to connect students and families to cost-effective services such as individual and group outpatient mental health services and support groups.

pooled.text: DEPRESSION SCREENING IN COLLEGE STUDENTS 5 The Importance of Screening and Early Identification of Depression in College Students In the United States, more than 33.3% of first-year college students reported symptoms that are consistent with a diagnosable mental health disorder, according to the American Psychological Association (Auerbach et al., 2018). Mental health problems among college students have consistently increased over time and it poses a threat to their health and academic performance (Lipson, Lattie, & Eisenberg, 2019). Identification of mental health disorders among college students have been overlooked. Depression is the second most common mental health disorder among college students in the United States (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students are a key population for determining the economic growth and success of the nation. Thus, primary healthcare providers are the front line to early screening and identification of depression amongst college students. Problem Statement The prevalence of depression has risen in the college population in the past decade. There is an estimation of 33.3% of college students exhibiting significant symptoms of depression, generalized anxiety disorder, or suicide ideation (Oswalt et al., 2018). Depression is one of the most common mental health conditions among college students. In the United States, approximately 26% of individuals ages 18 and older live with a diagnosable mental health disorder in a given year (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students with depression can experience a decrease in physical health, negatively impact mental health, hinder relationships, impede academic endeavors, and decrease quality of life (Pedrelli, Nyer, Yeung, Zulauf, & Wilens, 2015). Understanding these possible trends can be critical for providing equitable supports within a school. • For example, a school-wide screening effort may reveal that several classrooms may have a significant number of students with more intensive social- emotional-behavioral needs. • Rather than take the time to individually follow-up with every student, it may be helpful to provide classroom supports directly to the group to assess if there are larger group dynamics and classroom factors that can be addressed. • Screening data can help prioritize which students may benefit from more individualized services versus those who can have their needs addressed as part of a classroom intervention. Previous studies have considered a range of factors—such as financial aid (Dynarski, 1999) and academic and social involvement (Tinto, 1998)—that affect re maining in and completing college. Another important factor may be mental health. Mental disorders frequently have firs t onset shortly befo re or during the typical college age range (18-24) (Kessler et al., 2005), yet relatively little is known about the link between mental heal th and academic success in college.
